prompt: What is kickback?

The blade slowing down in thick stock

explanation: The back of the blade turns upward and toward you. Anything that lets the workpiece contact it gets launched.

prompt: What does a riving knife do?
choices: Keeps the kerf open behind the blade so the workpiece cannot pinch or contact the rising teeth
Guides the workpiece against the fence
Reduces splintering on the underside of the cut
Holds the blade guard in position
explanation: It is the single most effective anti-kickback device on the saw, which is why it stays on.

prompt: Why must you never use the rip fence and the miter gauge together for a crosscut?
choices: The offcut becomes trapped between blade and fence and gets thrown
The cut will be out of square
It dulls the blade prematurely
The miter gauge cannot reach the fence
explanation: The trapped offcut is the classic kickback setup. Use a stop block clamped ahead of the blade instead.

prompt: Where should you stand while ripping?

Directly behind the blade so the cut stays straight
At the outfeed end of the saw
As far to the left of the table as you can reach
explanation: Kickback travels straight back along the blade line. Do not be standing in it.

Only if the stock is under one inch wide

prompt: A cut binds partway through and the saw starts to bog down. What do you do?

Pull the workpiece back out of the blade quickly
Push harder to finish the cut
Let go of the workpiece and step back
explanation: Pulling back is what feeds the workpiece into the rising teeth. Letting go frees it to be thrown.

prompt: Why should you never cut freehand on a table saw - without the fence or the miter gauge?

The cut will not be straight enough for good work
It puts excessive wear on the arbor bearings
It is only unsafe on thin stock
explanation: This one is worth stating as an absolute rule rather than a judgment call.

Exactly level with the top of the stock
At least two inches above the stock
explanation: Lower means less exposed blade and a more downward cutting force. There is a genuine debate about full-height cutting; teach the conservative version in a shared shop.

A cut that relieves tension in the blade

prompt: After completing a miter saw cut, when may you raise the blade?

Immediately, as soon as the cut is through
As soon as you release the trigger

prompt: You need a very short piece cut on the miter saw. What is the safe approach?

Hold the short piece with your fingers close to the blade
Hold it with pliers
Freehand the cut quickly
explanation: Short offcuts near a miter saw blade are one of the most common ways people get hurt on the machine.

prompt: Why must you never crosscut - cut across the grain on a short piece - on a jointer?

It dulls the knives faster than face jointing

explanation: A jointer is for edges and faces along the grain, full stop.

prompt: You run a bowed board through the planer and it comes out the same thickness but still bowed. Why?

The planer knives are dull
You took too heavy a cut
The board was too short for the planer
explanation: This is the single most common misunderstanding about the jointer/planer pair and the reason the jointer exists.

prompt: Which stock must never go through the thickness planer?

explanation: Hidden metal destroys the knives and can throw fragments. Check reclaimed stock with a metal detector or do not run it.

prompt: On a router table, which way do you feed the workpiece relative to the bit?

With the bit's rotation, so the bit pulls the work through
Whichever direction is more comfortable
It only matters for bits over half an inch
explanation: Feeding with the rotation is a climb cut - the bit grabs the work and rockets it out of your hands.

prompt: What is a climb cut?

Routing uphill on a sloped surface
Taking multiple shallow passes instead of one deep one
Routing with the bit raised above the workpiece
explanation: Experienced woodworkers sometimes use light climb cuts deliberately. In a shared shop, teach it as a thing to recognize and avoid.

prompt: You need to remove a lot of material with a router bit. What is the right approach?

One full-depth pass with a slow feed rate
One full-depth pass with a fast feed rate
Two passes at full depth from opposite directions
explanation: Deep single passes are how bits break and workpieces get grabbed.

prompt: Why should you never wear gloves at the drill press?

Gloves reduce your grip on the workpiece
Gloves make the depth stop harder to set
Gloves are fine at the drill press
explanation: The counterintuitive one. Gloves protect you from splinters and burn you at rotating machinery.

prompt: You are drilling a hole through a small piece of metal or plastic. How should it be held?

Firmly by hand, with the other hand on the feed lever
Held with pliers
Held against the column for stability
explanation: When the bit breaks through, the workpiece spins. Small, smooth stock spins fastest and cuts worst.

prompt: You are about to use a large-diameter bit. What should happen to the spindle speed?

It should be increased - bigger bits need more speed
It makes no difference
It should be set to maximum for a cleaner hole
explanation: The rim of a large bit travels much further per revolution. Same rule as any rotating cutter.
